chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ibn Abi Nasr from Muhammad ibn Sama'ah from Zurarah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
I asked him about a man who said to his wife, 'You are forbidden to me,' so he (AS) said to me, 'If I had authority over him, I would strike his head.'

And I said to him, 'Allah (Exalted and Mighty) has made her permissible for you, so why did He not forbid her upon you? He did not add more than that he lied, claiming that what Allah made permissible is forbidden.' Therefore, neither divorce nor expiation enters upon him.
The saying of Allah (Exalted and Mighty), 'O Prophet, why do you forbid that which Allah has made permissible for you?'

So He placed expiation for him. He (AS) said, 'He only forbade upon himself his maid Mariyah and swore not to approach her. Therefore, He placed expiation for him for the oath, and did not place it for him for the prohibition.'

As for what he mentioned, may Allah have mercy on him, regarding the details of the divorce of the waiting period, we have presented it also in what preceded, and to add clarity to that is what we have narrated:
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling when a husband tells his wife 'You are forbidden to me' without a formal oath?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) distinguishes between a generic declaration of prohibition and a formal oath (Hilf), ruling that the former is merely a false claim without legal effect, while the latter incurs expiation as seen in the case of Mariyah bint Zam'ana. This hadith clarifies the jurisprudential nuance between Zihar, Talq, and simple verbal assertions, emphasizing that not every statement of 'forbidden' constitutes a binding religious decree. The Imam's reference to the Quranic narrative provides a precise exegetical boundary for applying kaffarah in marital disputes.
